facts.text: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills and one pumps it around the rest of the body.
A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance.
Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings — the only animal known to do so.
Sea otters sometimes hold paws while they sleep on the water, which keeps them from drifting apart.
Hummingbirds can hover in place and even fly backwards.
Koala fingerprints look so much like human fingerprints that they are hard to tell apart under a microscope.
Tardigrades survive drying out completely by entering a state called cryptobiosis, then revive when water returns.
A cow has one stomach divided into four compartments: the rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum.
A day on Venus (one full rotation, about 243 Earth days) is longer than its year (about 225 Earth days).
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
Saturn's average density is lower than that of water.
Venus is the hottest planet in the Solar System, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun — its thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere traps heat.
Jupiter spins faster than any other planet: a day there lasts about 10 hours.
The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth, by about 3.8 centimetres a year.
Olympus Mons on Mars is about two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.
A teaspoon of neutron-star material would weigh billions of tonnes on Earth.
Water expands by about 9% when it freezes, which is why ice floats.
A lightning bolt can heat the air around it to about 30,000 °C — several times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Light travels through a vacuum at 299,792,458 metres per second — exactly, because the metre is defined from it.
Botanically, a banana is a berry, but a strawberry is not.
Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth: a desert is defined by how little precipitation falls, not by heat.
Sharks are older than trees: the earliest sharks lived over 400 million years ago, before the first trees appeared.
Mount Everest is 8,848.86 metres tall, according to the joint survey by China and Nepal announced in 2020.
The Pacific Ocean covers more of Earth's surface than all of the land put together.
Australia is wider from east to west (about 4,000 km) than the Moon is across (about 3,474 km).
Russia spans eleven time zones.
Canada has the longest coastline of any country.
Despite the popular myth, the Great Wall of China cannot be seen from the Moon with the naked eye.
The word "algorithm" comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, a 9th-century Persian mathematician.
In 1843 Ada Lovelace published a method for computing Bernoulli numbers on Babbage's Analytical Engine — often called the first computer program.
In 1947 engineers working on the Harvard Mark II found a moth in a relay and taped it into their logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found".
Papermaking is traditionally credited to Cai Lun, an official of China's Han dynasty, around 105 CE.
The Rosetta Stone carries the same decree in three scripts, which let Jean-François Champollion decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs in 1822.
The Wright brothers' first powered flight, in December 1903, lasted 12 seconds.
Alexander Graham Bell received the patent for the telephone in 1876.
Movable type was invented in China by Bi Sheng around 1040, about four centuries before Gutenberg's press in Europe.
A googol is 10 to the power 100. The name was suggested by Milton Sirotta, the nine-year-old nephew of mathematician Edward Kasner.
There are infinitely many prime numbers — Euclid proved it more than 2,000 years ago.
In a group of just 23 people, the chance that two share a birthday is already over 50%.
1 + 2 + … + n equals n(n + 1) / 2, so the numbers from 1 to 100 add up to 5050.
Every position of a Rubik's Cube can be solved in 20 moves or fewer; this was proved by computer search in 2010.
In 628 CE the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote down rules for calculating with zero as a number.
Pi is irrational — its decimal digits never end or repeat. Johann Lambert proved this in 1761.
Hexagons divide a flat surface into equal cells with the least total wall length, which is why honeycomb cells are hexagonal. Thomas Hales proved this in 1999.
In 1936 Alan Turing proved that no general algorithm can decide, for every program and input, whether that program will eventually halt.
Edsger Dijkstra said he designed his shortest-path algorithm in about twenty minutes, at a café in Amsterdam in 1956, without pencil or paper.
Binary search was described in 1946, but Donald Knuth notes that the first published version correct for every array size did not appear until 1962.
In 2006 Joshua Bloch reported that Java’s Arrays.binarySearch could fail on huge arrays: (low + high) / 2 can overflow an int. The fix is low + (high - low) / 2.
Tony Hoare invented Quicksort in 1959, while working on machine translation as a visiting student in Moscow.
Merge sort was invented by John von Neumann in 1945.
Grace Hopper’s A-0 system of 1952 is often called one of the first compilers.
"Hello, world" as a first program comes from Brian Kernighan’s 1972 B tutorial and was made famous by The C Programming Language in 1978.
On 25 August 1991 Linus Torvalds announced the kernel that became Linux, calling it "just a hobby, won’t be big and professional".
Linus Torvalds wrote Git in 2005, after the Linux kernel project lost free use of its previous version-control tool.
Unix time counts seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC. A signed 32-bit counter runs out on 19 January 2038 — the "Year 2038 problem".
The first website, at info.cern.ch, was built by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN and went public in 1991.
ARPANET switched to TCP/IP on 1 January 1983 — a "flag day" often called the birth of the modern internet.
RSA encryption, published in 1977, is named after its inventors Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman.
In 1965 Gordon Moore observed that transistor counts on a chip doubled every year; in 1975 he revised it to about every two years.
Python is named after the comedy show Monty Python’s Flying Circus, not the snake.
Java was first called Oak, after a tree outside James Gosling’s office.
SQL began at IBM in 1974 as SEQUEL, designed by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce.
Ethernet was invented at Xerox PARC in 1973 by Robert Metcalfe and colleagues.
The first computer mouse, built in the 1960s for Douglas Engelbart’s team, had a wooden shell.
P versus NP is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems: a correct proof either way earns US$1 million.
In floating point, 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, because 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation.
In Java, Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) returns a negative number: −2,147,483,648 has no positive int counterpart in two’s complement.
Half a byte — 4 bits — is called a nibble, and it is exactly one hexadecimal digit.
